doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jazz Editions publishing, lost rights and getting them back
summary: Wallington's publishing deal for a dollar and 50% cost them for decades until an attorney recovered the copyrights.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Is it Billie who is his wife?
Billie was his wife.
Is he the guy who had Jazz Editions, Dad?
No.
No. Oh, ok...
Yes. Absolutely he was.
That’s what I was moving towards. Because then he offered to publish your music...
For a dollar.
It was an offer that seemed like a good idea at the time.
It took us years and years... In fact, we just got the rights back. We got an attorney to get it back.
Maybe he got Prestige to sign him, and then... Back then, I think, a lot of times when you were going to get a record deal, they’d also take publishing rights.
They’d moved to Florida, and we used to contact them in Florida, and they would never give the rights back.

When the copyright ran out and you tried to renew it yourself, they said someone else had already... So then he passed it on to... He has an uncle, Pete Figlia, who lives in Brooklyn or the Bronx... When we finally got an attorney...you got an attorney who immediately got them back. I don’t know why. We had other attorneys who said they couldn’t do it. But Roberta got the rights back. Because she discovered that he really would have owed us a huge amount of money. We were supposed to be collecting half of European royalties...
Mose has stated on public record that this is the case.
Oh. Anyway, she just wrote him a letter and he quickly said absolutely he would.
Just one of those old publishing deals, where it’s 50%, and in good faith you have to give for a dollar... I have the original contracts that say, like, a dollar.
Oh, you do?
Yeah. From 1957, and they were the first three albums worth of songs.
And the songs that were on there—“Parchman Farm” and “Young Man Blues,”
all the things that were so popular.
But I think back then, if you were going to get an album deal, somebody would say, “Oh, we’re going to publish.” It just kind of went hand-in-hand. And maybe...
We thought it was wonderful.
Yeah. It would have been if they’d paid...
Well, you did get six records out of it, and they were heard all over the world, and then it led to the events of the next 50-60 years.
I got some money out of Jazz Editions.
Yeah. 50%.
He would send a little note that said (?—21:06) 50%...
Anyway, we don’t have to go into...
Well, this is part of a musician’s life, too, and it’s an important part, being properly compensated for your musical production.
I think there was a time when that didn’t happen all the time.
I think there’s still a time when that doesn’t happen all the time.
Absolutely.
I think he’s very lucky to own 100% of all the copyrights now, which didn’t happen for...
